title: An Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Scan Method for Detecting Geographically Moving Disease Clusters
content:
Spatio-temporal disease clusters may change location as an outbreak spreads to adjacent areas. Many
common spatio-temporal scan statistics use fixed-shape regions (e.g., cylinders or ellipses) that do not
adapt to a changing cluster. We introduce MoveScan, a spatio-temporal scan statistic designed to detect moving disease clusters. MoveScan extends the prefiltered component-based greedy (PreCoG) scan
method to space-time data and retains units with a likelihood-ratio neighborhood statistic above a null
threshold. Adaptive temporal bridging then connects retained units in adjacent regions and consecutive
time periods only if the units are in different connected components. Using the bridged graph, a greedy
search produces candidate clusters. The threshold values are trained on null data independent of the
Monte Carlo reference. Under the null hypothesis, the test controls the Type I error in finite samples.
In simulation studies on moving clusters, MoveScan achieved the highest mean F1 score, mainly because
of its higher sensitivity. The score was 0.296 compared to 0.197–0.220 for the cylindrical, elliptical,
Takahashi, and GscanStat scans. In all 12 pairwise comparisons against the prism methods (four moving
cluster types, pooled across relative risks 2.0 and 2.5), the dataset-based 95% intervals were all positive.
The F1 score increased by 0.025 with bridging. For stationary clusters, the fixed-shape methods performed better. In the 2014–2015 Ebola outbreak in Sierra Leone, the top MoveScan cluster followed the
east-to-west spread of the outbreak. The top MoveScan cluster represented 25.6% of the person-weeks
and 93.6% of the excess cases. The top cluster of each of the prism methods represented a similar share
of the person-weeks but only 77% to 78% of the excess cases.
